SB 224 aims to ensure Utah's largest electric utility will remain heavily reliant on expensive and highly polluting coal power. Specifically, it prevents closure of Utah's Hunter and Huntington coal plants, even if operating them costs more than cleaner alternatives, and removes PacifiCorp's obligation to justify coal-related costs to regulators. Sophie Hayes of Utah Clean Energy stated: "Rather than charting a forward-looking path and embracing opportunities to lead in a new energy era, this bill commits Utahns to take on the cost and risk of these aging, costly resources."

SB153 requires most Utah voters' registration information to be public unless they are classified as "at-risk." Sen. John Johnson, R-North Ogden, sponsored SB153. He stated the measure "brings Utah law in line with federal law on voter transparency." The legislation passed largely along party lines, with two Senate Republicans opposing it and some Democrats voting in support.

SB153 — sponsored by Sen. John Johnson, R-North Ogden, and Rep. Trevor Lee, R-Layton — rolls back the previous "withheld" option that nearly 300,000 Utah voters have used to shield their registration records. Sponsor Sen. Johnson said the bill resolves a statutory conflict with the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) by restoring public access to voter registration records by default while retaining protections for individuals who meet a documented "at-risk" standard.

Utah's Energy Independence Amendments bill, SB224, was sponsored by Sen. Scott Sandall and keeps Utah's largest electric utility reliant on coal power, preventing closures of coal plants even when cleaner alternatives would cost less. Environmental groups expressed deep disappointment, stating the bill ensures Utah remains heavily dependent on aging, costly, and polluting coal resources.

Sen. John Johnson introduced Senate Bill 283, which would "prohibit universities from funding or maintaining offices focused on" diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives at Utah's public universities. Johnson stated the bill "seeks to ensure that public universities remain bastions of academic freedom and integrity, free from any ideological coercion." He expressed concern that "DEI bureaucracies within public universities may prioritize promoting particular political or social ideologies over academic rigor and intellectual diversity."

Johnson, though, views DEI programs with suspicion, worried they promote the interests of those they mean to benefit — students of color and others — at the expense of others. "How do we structure things so instead of creating a race war we actually create opportunities?" he said Monday.

Sen. John Johnson, R-North Ogden, sponsored legislation to prohibit funding of DEI offices in public higher education in a previous year. Johnson and Rep. Katy Hall co-authored a statement that "HB261 does not ban ideas, words from private individuals or academic topics. It bans compelled belief, and it bans discrimination based on personal identity characteristics."

SB 132 is a substantial bill that seeks to allow large new electricity loads of above 100 megawatts to procure new electricity supplies outside of the traditional Rocky Mountain Power process, with the aim to allow new customers, like potential data centers, to procure their energy needs. Under SB132, Rocky Mountain Power may individually contract with new customers requiring over 50 megawatts of power without affecting demands and rates for existing customers.

S.B. 132 Electric Utility Amendments 2025 General Session. Creates requirements for providing electrical service to large-scale electrical loads and establishes alternative processes for providing electric service to customers with large electrical loads. Senate passed SB132 on 2nd reading with 22 YES votes, 1 NO vote, and 6 OTHER votes; senators voting YES included Johnson among the 22.
